and the milk of mares they used to drink.
And the mark of distinction of the great emir among them
was this:
that the stirrup (or: stirrups) of his saddle was made of iron for him,
whereas all the rest made them of wood.
And in this very year, which is the year one thousand five hundred and fourteen of the Greeks [1203 AD],
Khan,
who is that Christian King John [Prester John],
was ruling over a certain tribe of the barbarian Huns that is called Kerait,
Chingiz
Khan was constantly going into his service.
And when he saw his brightness,
and that from day to day he was advancing,
he was envious of him,
and wished to seize him by treachery and put him to death.
Then two youths belonging to Ong Khan,
when they perceived the treachery,
informed Chingiz.
And at that very moment Chingiz informed his men,
and at night they moved from their tents and hid in ambushes.
And in the morning of that day, when Ong Khan fell upon the tents of the Tatars,
he found no one in them (in them {OCR?}). By a certain spring called Baljuna they encountered one another.
And the side of Chingiz was victorious,
and the side of Ong Khan was broken.
And again at other times they encountered one another,
until those of the house of Ong Khan completely perished,
and he too was killed,
and his wives and his sons and his daughters were taken captive.
And those two youths Chingiz Khan magnified,
and he established for them a law of freedom:
that in whatever plunder they might be present,
they and their sons for generation after generation,
no share for the king (or: kings) should be taken from them,
and without permission they might enter before the kings,
and however much they might offend, it should not be visited upon their head.
And the rest of the people who were with him in that battle
he exalted,
and made them nobles.
And because a clan of people of the Mongols who are called Oirats were with him,
and they more than the others showed prowess
and fought valiantly,
Chingiz Khan {OCR?} honored them,
and established for them a law
